rows.source: HSE refrigeration and cold-work safety
rows.verified: HSE identifies refrigeration failure modes including air ingress, corrosion, design faults, external events, fire or explosion and human error.

rows.source: HSE refrigeration and cold-work safety
rows.verified: Other failure modes include impact, impurities, maintenance faults, overheating, overpressurisation, structural failure, vibration and defective equipment.

rows.source: HSE refrigeration and cold-work safety
rows.verified: Air-ingress controls include operating procedures, reliable utilities, explosion relief, leak detection and training.

rows.source: HSE refrigeration and cold-work safety
rows.verified: Corrosion controls include material selection, coatings, inspection, corrosion monitoring and leak detection.

rows.source: HSE refrigeration and cold-work safety
rows.verified: Fire and explosion controls include suitable plant design, hazardous-area classification, fire protection, explosion relief and vent systems.

rows.source: HSE refrigeration and cold-work safety
rows.verified: Maintenance and impact controls can require inspections, permit-to-work systems, operating procedures, isolation and emergency response.

rows.source: HSE refrigeration and cold-work safety
rows.verified: Overheating and overpressure controls include alarms, trips, cooling, relief systems, ventilation, procedures and training.

rows.source: HSE refrigeration and cold-work safety
rows.verified: Chilled-food workplaces must meet food-hygiene needs while maintaining a reasonable workroom temperature or providing localised protection.

rows.source: HSE refrigeration and cold-work safety
rows.verified: Refrigeration risk depends on refrigerant, inventory, pressure, temperature, plant design, corrosion, ventilation, occupancy and emergency capability.

rows.source: HSE refrigeration and cold-work safety
rows.verified: Refrigeration evidence is system-, refrigerant-, failure-mode-, location- and operating-condition-specific and is not an exact parcel-level accident probability.

rows.source: HSE textiles and laundries respiratory controls
rows.verified: Textile and laundry workers can encounter dusts, fibres and chemical fumes that affect respiratory health.

rows.source: HSE textiles and laundries respiratory controls
rows.verified: Laundry and dry-cleaning hazards can include chlorine, hypochlorite, ammonia, sulphur dioxide and filter powders.

rows.source: HSE textiles and laundries respiratory controls
rows.verified: Laundry may be contaminated with hazardous material such as asbestos, requiring appropriate assessment and controls.

rows.source: HSE textiles and laundries respiratory controls
rows.verified: Textile process dust from materials such as cotton and wool can contribute to respiratory exposure.

rows.source: HSE textiles and laundries respiratory controls
rows.verified: Reactive dyes can present inhalation hazards, particularly during mixing or preparation without adequate ventilation.

rows.source: HSE textiles and laundries respiratory controls
rows.verified: Textile dust exposure can contribute to occupational asthma and respiratory irritation.

rows.source: HSE textiles and laundries respiratory controls
rows.verified: Laundry fumes can irritate the respiratory system when airborne chemical exposure is inadequately controlled.

rows.source: HSE textiles and laundries respiratory controls
rows.verified: Exposure should be controlled through ventilation, dust reduction and suitable respiratory protection where required.

rows.source: HSE textiles and laundries respiratory controls
rows.verified: Textile and laundry risk depends on fibre, chemical, contamination, process, ventilation, task duration, cleaning method and worker susceptibility.

rows.source: HSE textiles and laundries respiratory controls
rows.verified: Textile and laundry evidence is material-, process-, exposure- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level respiratory-disease probability.
